web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Machine — Segments, Customer Groups, and Real-World Workflows
question: How does Adobe's $23.77B FY2025 (and $26.6B FY2026-guided) revenue break down across clouds, customer groups, and geographies—and how do real customers actually use and pay for these tools?

epigraph.quote: Effective in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, we will combine our prior segments—Digital Media, Digital Experience and Publishing and Advertising—into a single operating and reportable segment.
epigraph.author: Adobe Inc., FY2025 Form 10-K (January 15, 2026)

web_blocks.text: The FY2026 Reporting Shift: From Three Segments to Two Customer Groups
web_blocks.title: The FY2026 Reporting Shift: From Three Segments to Two Customer Groups

web_blocks.html: To analyze Adobe in late 2026, you must track both its old three-segment map (through FY2025) and its new customer-group view (starting Q1 FY2026) [1, 3, 5]. In audited FY2025 (ended November 28, 2025), Adobe posted $23,769 million in total sales, up 10.5% YoY [1, 3]. Subscriptions generated $22,904 million (96.4%). Perpetual products added $325 million (1.4%), and services and other added $540 million (2.3%). Under the old segments, Digital Media (Creative Cloud and Document Cloud) brought in $17,650 million (74.3% of sales). Digital Experience delivered $5,860 million (24.7%), while legacy Publishing and Advertising added $256 million (1.1%) [1, 3].

In Q1 FY2026, Adobe merged its three legacy segments into one reporting unit to reflect cross-cloud AI suites like GenStudio and Acrobat Studio [1, 5]. Adobe now reports subscription revenue across two customer groups, while keeping Digital Media and Digital Experience subscriptions as extra disclosures [3, 6].
1. Creative & Marketing Professionals: This group pairs Creative Cloud (Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, After Effects, InDesign, Lightroom, Firefly, Frame.io, Substance 3D) with Experience Cloud (AEP, AEM, Analytics, Marketo Engage, Adobe Commerce, Workfront, GenStudio, Semrush). It posted $16,300 million in FY2025 (+11% YoY) and $4,650 million in Q3 FY2026 (+13% YoY; +12% CC) [3, 6].
2. Business Professionals & Consumers: This group pairs Document Cloud (Acrobat, Acrobat Sign, Acrobat Studio/AI Assistant) with consumer creative apps like Adobe Express and mobile Photography funnels. It posted $6,500 million in FY2025 (+15% YoY) and $1,910 million in Q3 FY2026 (+16% YoY; +15% CC) [3, 6].

web_blocks.takeaway: Subscriptions now make up 97.4% of quarterly sales (Q3 FY26). Business Professionals & Consumers (+16% YoY) outpaced Creative & Marketing Professionals (+13% YoY) as Acrobat AI and Express scaled.

web_blocks.text: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 1: Digital Media — Creative Cloud & Firefly
web_blocks.title: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 1: Digital Media — Creative Cloud & Firefly

web_blocks.html:
Who Buys & Pain Point: A 150-person global consumer-goods studio runs a 12-country holiday drink campaign. It needs 400 local product visuals, 30-second TV spots, print packaging files, and social cuts. Corporate legal must clear every asset for copyright safety.
Exact Products & Workflow: Art directors grade raw shots in Lightroom and Photoshop. They use Firefly Generative Fill to swap seasonal backdrops across regions, backed by licensed Adobe Stock training data and IP cover. Designers build vector logos in Illustrator and set print files in InDesign. Video editors cut 4K spots in Premiere Pro and add motion graphics in After Effects. They upscale clips with newly acquired Topaz Labs models and collect sign-offs through Frame.io [1, 18, 19]. Local marketers then adapt approved templates into social posts using Adobe Express.
Pricing & Commercials: Solo pros pay $69.99/month (annual plan) for Creative Cloud Pro with 4,000 monthly generative credits. Creative Cloud Standard costs $54.99/month with 25 monthly credits, while single apps start at $22.99/month [24]. Large teams sign Creative Cloud for Teams/Enterprise plans or three-year Enterprise Term License Agreements (ETLAs) that bundle Firefly Services APIs and Firefly Foundry custom models [1, 19].

web_blocks.text: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 2: Digital Media — Document Cloud & Acrobat Studio
web_blocks.title: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 2: Digital Media — Document Cloud & Acrobat Studio

web_blocks.html:
Who Buys & Pain Point: A mid-sized legal and buying team handles 15,000 vendor contracts, NDAs, and compliance filings each year. Checking 80-page redlines by hand burns staff hours. Split PDF viewers and e-signature tools also leave audit gaps.
Exact Products & Workflow: Staff already open contracts in free Acrobat Reader, part of a base opening over 400 billion PDFs a year [22]. Paid seats move up to Acrobat Pro and Acrobat Studio (launched August 2025) with Acrobat AI Assistant and PDF Spaces. A buyer drops five rival bids into one PDF Space and asks the Productivity Agent to compare indemnity and payment terms with exact page links. The buyer hides private pricing, turns the summary into a branded deck in Adobe Express, and sends the file for signing via Adobe Acrobat Sign [1, 6].
Pricing & Commercials: Acrobat Standard and Pro run about $12.99–$19.99 per user per month on annual plans, with AI Assistant add-ons near $4.99/month. This low-friction wedge lifted Business Professionals & Consumers sales 16% YoY to $1.91 billion in Q3 FY2026 [6].

web_blocks.text: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 3: Digital Experience — AEP, GenStudio & Semrush
web_blocks.title: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 3: Digital Experience — AEP, GenStudio & Semrush

web_blocks.html:
Who Buys & Pain Point: The CMO and CIO of a Fortune 500 retail bank or global airline face split customer data across web, mobile apps, call centers, and loyalty cards. In 2026, they face a fresh shift: shoppers now find financial products through chat LLMs instead of blue Google links.
Exact Products & Workflow: The firm runs Adobe Experience Platform (AEP) as its real-time Customer Data Platform (CDP), linking billions of clicks and CRM records into live profiles. Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) powers web and mobile storefronts. Adobe Journey Optimizer and Marketo Engage run tailored email, push, and B2B campaigns. Adobe GenStudio links Creative Cloud straight to Experience Cloud so teams brief, create, check, and track campaign variants fast. Newly bought Semrush and Adobe LLM Optimizer audit and boost how the bank appears inside AI search and shopping agents [1, 16]. Over 80% of AEP and AEM clients used agent tools by mid-FY2026 [6].
Pricing & Commercials: Unlike per-seat creative plans, Digital Experience uses multi-year enterprise deals priced by profiles, API calls, page views, and modules. Fortune 500 deals often run $500,000 to $10 million+ in annual contract value (ACV), billed upfront.

web_blocks.text: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 4: Publishing & Advertising (Legacy High-Margin Cash Cow)
web_blocks.title: Concrete Customer Walkthrough 4: Publishing & Advertising (Legacy High-Margin Cash Cow)

web_blocks.html:
Who Buys & Pain Point: Aerospace makers, commercial offset press OEMs, and defense firms need strict, zero-error manuals and print rendering. Modern consumer web apps cannot match that precision.
Exact Products & Workflow: An aircraft maker writes 10,000-page XML repair manuals in Adobe FrameMaker and builds safety courses in Adobe Captivate. Industrial presses run on licensed Adobe PostScript and PDF Print Engine firmware [1]. This unit made up just 1.1% of FY2025 sales ($256 million) and folded into Adobe's single segment in Q1 FY2026. It needs very little R&D and throws off high cash margins, though Adobe booked a $70 million goodwill writedown here in FY2026 [1].

book_paragraphs: If you ask ten people what Adobe does, nine of them will say Photoshop and PDFs. That answer is accurate, yet it misses nearly a quarter of the company's revenue and the entire strategic reorganization Adobe executed in fiscal 2026. To analyze Adobe like an institutional owner, you have to understand both the legacy three-segment map and the new two-customer-group lens that management adopted at the start of fiscal 2026.

Start with the audited fiscal 2025 foundation. Out of $23.77 billion in total revenue, an extraordinary 96.4 percent—$22.90 billion—came from recurring subscriptions. By the third quarter of fiscal 2026, subscriptions climbed even higher to 97.4 percent of quarterly revenue. Under the legacy structure, Digital Media—housing Creative Cloud and Document Cloud—generated $17.65 billion, or 74.3 percent of total sales. Digital Experience generated $5.86 billion, or 24.7 percent, while legacy Publishing and Advertising contributed $256 million, roughly 1.1 percent. Geographically, Adobe is globally diversified: the Americas contributed 59.4 percent of fiscal 2025 revenue, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa delivered 26.5 percent, and Asia-Pacific generated 14.1 percent.

In Q1 FY2026, Adobe formally collapsed those three legacy segments into a single reportable segment. Management did this because generative AI has blurred the boundary between creating an image, editing a document, and launching a marketing campaign. Today, Adobe tracks subscription performance across two customer groups. The first, Creative and Marketing Professionals, brings together pro creative apps and enterprise Experience Cloud; it generated $16.30 billion in fiscal 2025 and $4.65 billion in Q3 FY2026, growing 13 percent year over year. The second, Business Professionals and Consumers, pairs Document Cloud with Express and consumer mobile apps; it generated $6.50 billion in fiscal 2025 and $1.91 billion in Q3 FY2026, growing a faster 16 percent year over year.

Numbers only come alive when you trace real customers through the software. Consider first a global consumer-goods brand launching a twelve-country holiday campaign through Creative Cloud. Its creative studio needs four hundred localized product visuals, broadcast video commercials, print packaging files, and social cutdowns—and corporate legal refuses to touch unindemnified AI art generators for fear of copyright lawsuits. Photographers grade product shots in Lightroom and retouch them in Photoshop, using Firefly Generative Fill to swap seasonal backdrops cleanly with commercial IP indemnification. Packaging designers build vector logos in Illustrator and print mechanicals in InDesign. Video editors cut commercials in Premiere Pro, add motion graphics in After Effects, upscale archival footage using Topaz Labs models, and collect executive sign-offs in Frame.io. Regional marketers then localize approved templates inside Adobe Express. Individual pros pay $69.99 a month for Creative Cloud Pro with 4,000 generative credits, or $54.99 for Standard with just 25 credits, while enterprises sign three-year term agreements that bundle seats with Firefly API capacity.

Now walk into a second building: a corporate legal and procurement team handling fifteen thousand vendor contracts a year. Every employee already opens PDFs in free Acrobat Reader—part of an installed base opening more than four hundred billion PDFs annually. That ubiquity is Adobe's secret weapon. When the legal team upgrades to Acrobat Pro and Acrobat Studio, a procurement manager drops five competing supplier bids into a single PDF Space and instructs Acrobat AI Assistant to compare indemnity clauses with exact page citations. Once finalized, the contract routes directly through Adobe Acrobat Sign for audited execution. At $13 to $20 per seat plus a $5 AI Assistant add-on, Document Cloud is a quiet juggernaut driving the fastest subscription growth in Adobe's portfolio.

Third, step into the boardroom of a Fortune 500 retail bank or global airline buying Digital Experience. Their problem is not making one pretty poster; it is orchestrating billions of personalized customer interactions across web, mobile, and email without violating privacy laws. They deploy Adobe Experience Platform as their real-time customer data hub, run their digital storefronts on Adobe Experience Manager, and automate campaigns through Journey Optimizer and Marketo Engage. In 2026, two new pieces lock this enterprise stack together. GenStudio bridges Creative Cloud directly into Experience Cloud so marketers can spin up on-brand campaign variants at scale. Meanwhile, Semrush—acquired for $1.9 billion in April 2026—pairs with Adobe LLM Optimizer to measure and improve how the bank's brand appears when consumers ask AI assistants for product recommendations. Unlike per-seat creative subscriptions, these multi-year enterprise deals run from half a million to over ten million dollars per year, billed upfront.

Finally, do not overlook the tiny 1.1 percent legacy tail in Publishing and Advertising. Aerospace manufacturers still author ten-thousand-page aircraft maintenance manuals in FrameMaker, and industrial offset printers still run on licensed PostScript and PDF Print Engine firmware. It is no longer a growth engine—Adobe even took a $70 million goodwill impairment there in fiscal 2026—yet it remains a high-margin reminder of how long technical standards endure once embedded in mission-critical workflows.

Look even closer at the pricing architecture Adobe introduced inside Creative Cloud in mid-2025, because it tells you how management thinks about monetizing AI without triggering wholesale churn. Rather than forcing every subscriber onto one flat rate, Adobe split its flagship bundle into two tiers: Creative Cloud Standard at $54.99 per month on an annual commitment, capped at just 25 monthly generative AI credits, and Creative Cloud Pro at $69.99 per month, granting 4,000 monthly generative credits plus full Firefly web and video capabilities. That $15 monthly spread is a classic price-discrimination staircase. Casual users who barely touch generative fill stay anchored on Standard, while heavy agency professionals—who burn through 25 credits in a single afternoon—naturally self-select into Pro or buy standalone Firefly credit packs.

The same layered monetization logic runs through Adobe's geographic footprint. In the Americas—nearly 60 percent of revenue—growth is anchored by multi-year Fortune 500 ETLAs, federal and state government document modernization, and university campus licenses. In EMEA, representing 26.5 percent of sales, global ad holding companies and luxury retail brands drive heavy Experience Cloud and GenStudio adoption, though currency swings routinely add or subtract hundreds of millions from year-end ARR revaluations (including the $460 million upward FX revaluation entering fiscal 2026). Meanwhile, Asia-Pacific at 14.1 percent of revenue is Adobe's fastest-expanding region, where mobile-first creators in India, Japan, and Southeast Asia enter through Adobe Express and Lightroom Mobile before graduating into paid subscriptions.

Equally important is how the two customer groups balance each other's risk profile. Creative and Marketing Professionals is the profit powerhouse at $16.30 billion in fiscal 2025 subscription revenue, but it sits directly in the crosshairs of generative AI disruption and agency seat optimization. Business Professionals and Consumers, at $6.50 billion in fiscal 2025 and growing 16 percent in Q3 FY2026, behaves more like a ubiquitous enterprise utility: every law firm, bank, hospital, and government agency runs on PDFs, and embedding conversational AI directly into Acrobat Studio turns a static file viewer into an active knowledge-work workspace.

Put all four workflows together and you see Adobe's true economic identity. It is not merely a collection of creative apps; it is a tollbooth on the global content supply chain—from the moment a designer opens a blank canvas or a lawyer opens a PDF, to the millisecond an enterprise marketing engine serves a personalized webpage or tracks its visibility inside an AI answer engine. The critical question for the chapters ahead is how efficiently that tollbooth converts revenue into cash, and whether nimble browser-native and AI-native challengers can route traffic around it.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why the Segment Merger Matters
book_callouts.text: Be alert whenever a large software company reorganizes its reporting segments. Consolidating Digital Media and Digital Experience into a single reportable segment reflects genuine cross-cloud convergence around GenStudio and AI agents—but it also reduces standalone visibility into Creative Cloud versus Document Cloud growth. As an analyst, always track the supplemental disclosures and Total ARR alongside the new customer groups.
